nodes.label: Women are Always on the Move
nodes.text:
WOMEN ENGAGE IN DIFFERENT TYPES of work and mobility that inform their journeys through life. They work at home, in the fields, in the workshops, in big cities, small towns, or in other countries. Their work and their movement traverse different spaces, reassembling their relationships as they become part of many other people’s lives. This exhibition introduces glimpses into the lives of 21 women – women, who have worked and moved as doctors, maids, actresses, students, accountants, filmmakers, embroiderers, teachers, artists, and as mothers, daughters, mentors and friends. They live in Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon and Denmark, yet their lives invite us to travel across many more spaces, peoples, and times, and inspire us to rethink familiar meanings and assumptions about women, mobility and work.

This exhibition is based on interviews with these diverse women. We are a group of researchers, archivists, museum professionals and young people in these professions, who all share an interest in telling and sharing the stories of these women, whose inspiring tales should be kept and remembered for generations to come. We invite you on a journey through their lives to see how they have moved and for what different reasons. We shed light on the effect that these movements and their work have on their relationships with the people around them and delve into their different types of work to see how they contribute to not only their own lives but also to their families, friends, co-workers and to society.

nodes.label: On Mobility
nodes.text:
Sometimes women move by accident, sometimes by choice, and sometimes by force. Many never stop moving despite the obstacles on the road, with possibilities and challenges always as a potential along the way. Their movements have shaped their lives and those of others, leaving traces on who and how they are.

Nadia Safwat (b. 1986) travelled with her family who settled in Denmark to work, ambivalently shrouding her relations to her family in Cairo. The Nakba forced Im Ibrahim (b.1927) to flee her hometown Jaffa when it was invaded by Israeli soldiers in 1948. While fleeing on foot, she carried her embroidered costumes as inseparable parts of her being that cannot be left behind. Hind Rostum(1931 -2011) became an actress at the age of 15. As a child, she travelled together with her father whose changing professions took them all over Egypt. Her work later would take her through many more places and relationships. Safeya Gamal (b.
1934) was one of the Nubians who were forced to move when the Aswan High Dam was built. She felt as if this was their judgement day. Wedad Mitri (1927 - 2007) came into teaching by chance. Since beginning her career she has moved to many places, and inspired many of her students. Widad Al Orfali (b. 1929) opened the first private gallery in Iraq in the 1980s. When the war began in 2003, she was forced to leave her gallery and her paintings behind.

nodes.label: On Work
nodes.text:
Work is a complex experience that marks women’s worlds. But what is work and how does it become a central part of a life project? What is recognized as work, what has to be rendered invisible to be able to fend for one’s life, and how are our bodies and affects moulded with work rhythms, routines, tools and corporeal traces? The stories of the women presented here urge us to rethink the meanings, worlds and effects of work. Work traverses women’s lives from early years to late moments of being; work experiences inhabit our worlds at home, in the fields, factories, banks, schools, workshops, gas stations, galleries, and movie screens. The women you are about to meet have worked hard all their lives in many different spaces and times. Their experiences encourage us to reflect on what lies in and outside of work, how work spills over other domains of being, and how work has exuded pride and shame, happiness and sadness, leaving unmistakable marks on our bodies and the worlds we inhabit.

Instead of learning how to read and write, Rawya Mohammed (b. 1978) learned the craft of pottery already at age 12. Since then, her work has inspired many other women to take up pottery and her patterns have forever changed the face of pottery in Fayoum in Egypt. Kawkab Hifni Nassef (1905 - 1999) was the first woman to ever run a hospital in Egypt. Balsam Abou Zour’s (b. 1982) village did not approve of her work as a painter, but after a visit from her teachers, her fate changed. When she opened her first art exhibition, her entire village attended in celebration.

nodes.label: Hind Rustum Advertisement
nodes.text: Al-Kawakib is an Egyptian arts magazine known for its coverage of Egyptian film. Established in 1932 as a weekly by Lebanese brothers Emil and Shokry Zidan and issued by Dar al-Hilal publishing house, Al-Kawakib became a monthly from 1949 to 1954. Since then the magazine, still in publication, has been a weekly publication. Heavily illustrated and considered a "celebrity" magazine for its focus on movie stars, Al-Kawakib offers rich documentation for the history of Egyptian cinema.

nodes.label: On Reassembling Relations
nodes.text: Relationships are Reassembled along the roads of women’s lives, connecting and disconnecting them with people and spaces in constantly evolving life projects. From friends, neighbours, mentors, to colleagues, wives, daughters, and role models, women reconstitute their worlds for better and for worse. But the most valuable relationships can come from somewhere completely unexpected – be it from your students, neighbours, friends or from other women you live with. The photographs and other memorable traces of relationships that we present here, reveal how people and objects along life journeys make who and how we are constantly in a process of becoming.

nodes.label: The Nubian Exodus
nodes.text:
The Aswan High Dam is an engineering project constructed in 1970 at the border of Egypt and Sudan. The dam provides hydroelectricity, irrigation control, and security from floods and droughts to farmers along the banks of the Nile. Upon completion, it formed a large reservoir which would come to be known as Lake Nasser.

While the project accomplished its initial goals, the flooding forcibly displaced a significant population of Nubians — at least 90,000 — from their historic farmlands and cultural sites. While many Nubians were sent to settlements near Kom Ombo, many travelled to Cairo and Alexandria in search of work. The creation of these dams not only directly displaced Nubians but flooded previously fertile soil historically used by Nubian farmers.

nodes.label: The Palestinian Exodus
nodes.text:
Al-Nakba, or "the catastrophe," refers to the violent expulsion of Palestinians from their homes by Israeli forces from 1947–1949. The Nakba occurred prior to and following the passing of Resolution 181 by the UN General Assembly, which ruled that Palestine be separated into two states, one Arab and one Jewish.

Prior to the proposed implementation of the two-state solution, Israeli forces enacted Plan Dalet, beginning a widespread campaign of terror and violence against Palestinians. On April 9 of 1948, Zionist forces killed more than 100 Palestinians in what would later be known as the Deir Yassin massacre.

By the end of the 1948 war, Israel had seized control of 78% of the land. The war was accompanied by the mass displacement of the Palestinian population: approximately half of all Palestinians, between 750,000 and 900,000 people, were expelled from their homes, laying the foundation for a refugee crisis that persists today.

nodes.label: Nada Abdel Rahman's Keys
nodes.text: When Nada Abdel Rahman (b. 1986), moved to Cairo in 2014, she shared a flat with nineteen other women. The twenty women, who were in their 20s, 30s, and 40s, were all migrants, coming from various towns across Egypt. By sharing food and stories, Nada started building bonds with her flat mates. "I thought that breaking bread together would bring the girls closer to each other. I started thinking that all we have is each other." Nada, 2016. Through her new friends, Nada heard of a feminist filmmaking workshop where she directed her first short film.

nodes.label: Safeya's Basket
nodes.text: Safeya Gamal was born in 1934 in Cairo to a Nubian family. Safeya spent most of her childhood in Nubia where she went to primary school. Like other girls growing up in Nubia at the time, Safeya learned how to weave baskets, plates, mats, fans and jars from straw. Perceived primarily as brides-to-be, the girls were told that perfecting basket-making would help them get married. Safeya made this plate herself. At the age of sixteen, Safeya was married and moved to Cairo in 1948. Safeya's mother taught her the Nubian language and gave her this leather wallet (left), a family heirloom which the mother herself inherited. Now, the wallet belongs to Safeya's grandson.

nodes.label: Wedad's Postcards
nodes.text: Wedad Metri (1927-2007) worked as a teacher in public schools outside of Cairo during the 1950s. Wedad became a mentor for many of her young students. Her private collected, hosted at the Women and Memory Forum, includes many postcards she received from her devoted students over the years.

nodes.label: Reem and Shahinda
nodes.text:
Four Women of Egypt (1997) is a documentary film directed by Tahani Rached that follows the lives of four prominent Egyptian women who engaged in the women's movement throughout and following the Nasser era (1952–1970). The women, alike in their involvement with female-driven activity and broader anticolonial pursuits, notably differed in their ideological positions, with each woman possessing a unique orientation to socialism, feminism, Islamism, and secularism.

Central to the women's interactions with political movements is class positionality and proximity to privilege. Early on in the film, Amina Rachid reflects on an experience where a little girl attacked her with stones because Rachid's grandfather, Egyptian prime minister Ismail Sidqi, had signed a treaty with the British: 'The big house, the poor neighbours. So, this political drama was for me a shock and an awakening. In our big house we spoke French, and Arabic only with the servants. The bitter truth of being the ruling class. Outside the gate, a traitor.'

nodes.label: Gam3aya
nodes.text: The gameya is form of rotating savings and credit association. It is a small group, often ranging from 10 to upwards of 30 people, who contribute to a money sharing pool on a monthly basis. Each month this group gathers money and distributes it to each member within the group in turn, allowing for larger expenditures on tuition fees, medical expenses, or small business investments without the need to rely on formal banks. While both men and women often participate in gameyas, they are more frequently operated and organized by women. Similarly, many women operate in the role of moneykeepers, informally storing savings given to them by community members.

nodes.label: May Kassicieh's Embroidery
nodes.text: May Kassicieh was born in Amman, Jordan in 1952. She currently lives in the United States of America. May cherishes this handkerchief as it is the first piece of embroidery she made as a child. "To me, embroidery represents a permanent sense of self. Despite leaving my homeland, moving from country to country, city to city, embroidery is a craft that allows me to transcend location, being, and even identity. There is a sense of permanence to it; it can't be washed away or removed. Embroidery is a craft that was passed down to me from my mother, and to her from her mother, and so on. It's a story and an identity and a way of life that taught me, and all of us, the importance of patience and the intricacy of dedication." May Kassicieh, 2016.

nodes.label: Saadeya's Wedding Ring
nodes.text: Wedding Photo of Saadeya Hussein in Cairo, 1990s. Saadeya Hussein (b. 1975) currently works as a house-maid. "Before getting married, I had to work to pay for setting up the new household. My mother did not have an income... she used to tell me that I am the hands and legs of the household. Without working, I would not have been able to feed my children." Saadeya, 2016.

nodes.label: Im Ibrahim's Embroidery
nodes.text:
Tatreez, a form of traditional Palestinian embroidery, encompasses the colorful stitching found on Palestinian textiles. Practiced for centuries, evidence of its use goes as far back as 1283 CE. Tatreez can depict anything from the natural environment to geometric patterns and common objects. The styles, patterns and symbols used prominently on the Palestinian thobe, or woman's dress, represent the wearer's personal connections, religious beliefs, or relationships to different areas within Palestine.

Following the Nakba, access to the materials required for these textiles became extremely difficult to procure. While some regional variety was lost, as displaced persons shared techniques, tatreez and thobe became symbols of resistance against cultural erasure. In particular, during the first intifada, tatreez was used to embroider the Palestinian flags into keffiyeh and thobe. For the Palestinian diaspora, embroidery connects generations across disparate geographies through a practice tied not just to livelihood, but resistance and collective identity.

nodes.label: Mariam's Soap & Oil
nodes.text: "There is a certain smell I associate (with home)... a smell of the clothes that my grandmother washed." Mariam Safwat (b. 1992), 2016.

nodes.label: Widad al-Orfali Biography
nodes.text:
Widad al-Orfali was born in Baghdad, Iraq in 1929. She currently lives in Amman, Jordan. Widad's many travels inspired her paintings that were exhibited in Germany, Jordan, Lebanon, the UAE and the USA. In addition to being an accomplished painter, Widad has been a documentarian of Iraqi cultural heritage and traditional crafts.

al-Orfali opened the first private gallery in Iraq in the 1980s. Over the years, this gallery became an essential player in the Iraqi cultural scene by supporting emerging artists, musicians, and singers. However, sustaining the gallery became challenging as audiences diminished under the Embargo of 1990. Speaking of the meager public visiting the gallery, al-Orfali said, the "decided to launch a bullet of mercy on the Orfali Gallery." Widad, Swalif, 2015.

When the war began in 2003, she was forced to leave her country and her paintings behind. Afterwards, Widad stopped painting and channeled her creative forces into music. She released an album, Rhythms of Arabia, in 2010. In 2015, Widad published her autobiography Swalif.

nodes.label: Biography of Wedad Mitri
nodes.text:
The Algerian Revolution (1954–1962), characterized by its unabashed rejection of France's "civilizing" objectives in its colonies, its radical Leninist-Maoist politics, and ambitions toward decolonization and self-determination, represented a key expression of the solidarity between Arab nations and other countries within the Global South that emerged from collective disillusionment and frustration with Western institutions and hierarchies.

Nasser's identity as a champion of Pan-Arabism was exemplified in his unabashed support of the FLN, to which he provided ideological as well as material and logistical support. Notably, he used "Voice of the Arabs," the aptly named Egyptian radio station, to disseminate anti-Anglo-American, pro-Pan-Arab rhetoric that urged citizens across the region to recenter Arab identity as a means of resisting imperial imposition.

nodes.label: Biography of Im Ibrahim
nodes.text:
Ruqaya el-Santarisy "Im Ibrahim" was born in Jaffa, Palestine in 1927. Im Ibrahim currently lives in Amman, Jordan, where she runs her own embroidery workshop.

In 1948, Im Ibrahim fled her hometown with her husband, who was trained as a teacher. After three years of financial hardship in Damascus, Syria, Im Ibrahim and her family migrated to Jordan. Im Ibrahim, her husband, and their eight children made a home for themselves in Amman. By the 1950s, the resourceful Im Ibrahim turned her embroidery skills, which she learned at the age of 10, into an income-generating activity. In addition to training several generations of embroiderers over the following decades, Im Ibrahim has become known for re-fashioning the embroidery of cushions.

In recent years, Im Ibrahim's workshop sales have been declining due to decreasing demand on embroidery in contemporary markets.

nodes.label: AAWC
nodes.text:
Hosted in Lahore, Pakistan from January 19-25 of 1931, the All Asian Women’s Congress brought together delegates from across Asia to build a transnational feminist movement. With 26 delegate representatives from India, Afghanistan, Burma, Ceylon, Japan, and Persia in addition to 1200 observers, the conference sought to create a feminist movement from the perspective of non-Western women. While the role of Western feminists was acknowledged, the main concern, voiced by one conference organizer, stated that colonialism and geography limited “we only know of those who come to us” (Nijhhawan 17). Thus, the conference sought to de-imperialize feminism by creating a shared regional identity. While men and women from Europe and America were permitted to attend the conference, they were barred from speaking until the fourth day of assembly.

The conference proposed six goals: the promotion of a shared consciousness of unity amongst Asian women, appreciation of the positive qualities of their civilizations, review and remediation of traditional society, the sifting of Western influence for appropriate adoption, the sharing of national data, and world peace.

Though not directly related, these conferences served as a link in the broader chain of formal women’s networks in Asia which stood against conventional Western narratives around feminism. Hanifa Khouri would serve as one of the organizers of a following conference, the Eastern Women’s Congress in Tehran. Nour Hamada, a prominent Druze activist from Mount Lebanon, advised the planning of the All Asian Women’s Congress (Hannun 13). Her organization, the General Union for Syrian Women, was later responsible for organizing the Eastern Women’s Congress in 1932.

nodes.label: Nadia and Zeynab's Suitcase
nodes.text: Zeynab and Nadia Safwat's suitcase is a portable archive that travels with the exhibition. Inside, family photographs from Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and Denmark sit beside silver jewelry, embroidered textiles, and a Hamsa-engraved keepsake — small objects whose weight is the relationships they carry across distance. Open the case to scroll through every item at full size.
